title: Enhanced mTORC1 signaling and protein synthesis in pathologic α-synuclein cellular and animal models of Parkinson’s disease

venue.name: Science Translational Medicine
venue.publisher: American Association for the Advancement of Science

abstract: Pathologic α-synuclein plays an important role in the pathogenesis of α-synucleinopathies such as Parkinson's disease (PD). Disruption of proteostasis is thought to be central to pathologic α-synuclein toxicity; however, the molecular mechanism of this deregulation is poorly understood. Complementary proteomic approaches in cellular and animal models of PD were used to identify and characterize the pathologic α-synuclein interactome. We report that the highest biological processes that interacted with pathologic α-synuclein in mice included RNA processing and translation initiation. Regulation of catabolic processes that include autophagy were also identified. Pathologic α-synuclein was found to bind with the tuberous sclerosis protein 2 (TSC2) and to trigger the activation of the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) complex 1 (mTORC1), which augmented mRNA translation and protein synthesis, leading to neurodegeneration. Genetic and pharmacologic inhibition of mTOR and protein synthesis rescued the dopamine neuron loss, behavioral deficits, and aberrant biochemical signaling in the α-synuclein preformed fibril mouse model and Drosophila transgenic models of pathologic α-synuclein-induced degeneration. Pathologic α-synuclein furthermore led to a destabilization of the TSC1-TSC2 complex, which plays an important role in mTORC1 activity. Constitutive overexpression of TSC2 rescued motor deficits and neuropathology in α-synuclein flies. Biochemical examination of PD postmortem brain tissues also suggested deregulated mTORC1 signaling. These findings establish a connection between mRNA translation deregulation and mTORC1 pathway activation that is induced by pathologic α-synuclein in cellular and animal models of PD.

narrative:
Short impact summary

This 2023 Science Translational Medicine article has already shown strong scholarly traction, with 51 OpenAlex citations and a field- and year-normalized standing in the top 10% of its cohort. Its influence is visible not only in citation volume but also in downstream reuse, with 52 documented reuses across articles, preprints, reviews, and book chapters, indicating that the paper has entered an active research conversation on Parkinson’s disease mechanisms.

Full narrative

The article addresses a central problem in Parkinson’s disease research: how pathologic α-synuclein disrupts proteostasis and contributes to neuronal toxicity. Using complementary proteomic approaches in cellular and animal models, the study links α-synuclein pathology to enhanced mTORC1 signaling and increased protein synthesis, helping clarify a mechanism that is relevant to neurodegeneration and therapeutic targeting. Its publication in a high-profile translational venue and its association with a Dryad dataset also support its role as a reusable research resource.

The citation record suggests that the paper has been taken up rapidly and broadly within the neuroscience and neurodegeneration literature. Citations are concentrated in 2024 through 2026, and the citing venues include journals and preprint servers that are prominent in this area, such as bioRxiv, Neuron, Molecular Neurobiology, Frontiers in Neuroscience, and Research Square. The themes of citing works align closely with the paper’s core contribution, especially Parkinson’s disease mechanisms, autophagy, lysosomal dysfunction, and PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling.

Reuse patterns reinforce that this is not just a cited paper but one that has been incorporated into multiple forms of scholarly output. The downstream record includes many article-level reuses, along with preprints, reviews, and book chapters, suggesting that the study’s findings are being used both to frame new experimental work and to contextualize broader mechanistic discussions. The presence of an indexed article mention in Europe PMC also indicates continued visibility in biomedical literature infrastructure.

Overall, the record shows a work with clear early-to-midterm scholarly influence in a highly active field. The evidence points to substantive academic uptake rather than broad public discourse: there are citations, reuse, and disciplinary follow-on work, but no recorded event-based mentions in the available archive. In that context, the article’s impact is best understood as mechanistic and methodological influence within Parkinson’s disease and neurodegeneration research, especially around α-synuclein biology and mTORC1-regulated proteostasis.
